chunks: "Pretty much anything that is the same operation applied to a huge amount of independent data.

The headline example today is machine learning: training and inference are dominated by big matrix multiplies and convolutions, which are exactly the high-arithmetic-intensity, regular, parallel workloads a GPU is built for, and modern GPUs even have tensor cores for it.
Scientific simulation is another: molecular dynamics, fluid dynamics, N-body, weather.
Then image and video processing, signal processing like FFTs, Monte Carlo methods in finance, hash computation and cryptographic brute-force, genomics alignment, and database scans and sorts.
The why is the same in every case. The work is data-parallel, so thousands of threads can run without talking to each other.
Memory access is regular, so the wide memory bus is used well.
And either the arithmetic per byte is high, so the FLOPS get used, or the job just streams data, so the huge memory bandwidth, ten times a CPU's, is what helps.
It doesn't help for things like pointer-chasing, a lot of branching, small problems, or jobs where moving data over PCIe takes longer than the compute."
